> A custom handheld retro gaming console powered by an ESP32 NodeMCU, featuring a 1.3" IPS color display (240x240 ST7789 via SPI), 8 tactile buttons, and an 8-bit piezo buzzer. Includes a custom 2-layer PCB designed in KiCad and playable retro games (Snake, Flappy, Tetris, Pong, Wolf 3D) written in C++.

## Design

### 2026-10-05: ### Concept sketching and parts sourcing for week 1

**1.5h**

### Concept sketching and parts sourcing for week 1

Today I started working on week 1 of Half-Life. My goal is to design a small retro gameboy console around an ESP32.

I first sat down with a sheet of paper to figure out the dimensions and layout. I put the 1.3 inch SPI display in the upper center, a d-pad on the left, tilted A and B buttons on the right, and start plus select buttons right below. I also sketched an SPDT slide switch on the side for power and left space for a speaker grill for the buzzer.

After that I spent most of the session sourcing parts to stay below the $30 budget limit. Picking the buzzer took some time because most cheap listings on AliExpress were active buzzers, but I specifically needed a passive 12mm one so I can modulate different frequencies in code for game tones. I got the ST7789 display, the buzzer, and some monolithic 100nF caps on AliExpress.

For the board fabrication I set up JLCPCB for 5 boards.

Overall I got the layout sketched, figured out the basic pin connections, and filled out the whole BOM within the budget. Next I will boot up KiCad and draw the schematic.

### 2026-10-06: What I did:

**2h**

What I did:

Updated the README, overhauled the BOM, and sorted out part sourcing after the PCB export.

Details:

    - Exported the final Gerbers and drill files in KiCad and cleaned up the repo documentation (wich took a while because im a first-timer with KiCAD).

      - Hit a massive issue with the AliExpress checkout: because of the new EU customs reform, they added massive toll wich i had to evade.

   - Realized I already have passive buzzers, 2.54mm female headers, and spare 100nF (104) ceramic caps lying around, so I cut those entirely from the purchase list to save money.

   - Recalculated the BOM with verified vendors so the project stays within the limit. Next step is optimizing my PCB design and setting sail to the writing of the firmware/software.
